title: Explain the Singleton pattern and the thread-safe ways to implement it in Java — eager initialization (simple, not lazy), lazy with a synchronized getter (lazy but locks on every call), double-checked locking (needs a volatile instance to avoid returning a partially-constructed object), the Bill Pugh initialization-on-demand holder idiom (lazy + thread-safe via class loading, no synchronization), and an enum singleton (concise, with free serialization-/reflection-safety) — and which are preferred (Bill Pugh or enum)?
shortTitle: Explain the Singleton pattern and the thread-safe ways to implement it
topicTitle: Explain the Singleton pattern and the thread-safe ways to implement it in Java

s1_definition.profdef: The Singleton pattern ensures a class has exactly one instance across the whole application and provides a single global access point to it. In a multi-threaded program you must guarantee that two threads cannot create two instances at the same time. Java offers several thread-safe approaches: eager initialization, a synchronized getter, double-checked locking with a volatile field, the Bill Pugh initialization-on-demand holder idiom, and the enum singleton. The Bill Pugh holder and the enum are the preferred approaches because they are correct, lazy, and simple.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has exactly one central vault for the whole bank. There is no second vault, and every branch that needs the vault uses the same one through a single controlled door. If two staff members tried to build a vault at the very same moment, you could end up with two vaults, which must never happen. Making sure only one vault ever exists, even when many staff rush the door together, is exactly what thread-safe Singleton creation guarantees.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Singleton pattern ensures a class has exactly one instance across the whole application and provides a single global access point to it. In a multi-threaded program you must guarantee that two threads cannot create two instances at the same time. Java offers several thread-safe approaches: eager initialization, a synchronized getter, double-checked locking with a volatile field, the Bill Pugh initialization-on-demand holder idiom, and the enum singleton. The Bill Pugh holder and the enum are the preferred approaches because they are correct, lazy, and simple.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has exactly one central vault for the whole bank. There is no second vault, and every branch that needs the vault uses the same one through a single controlled door. If two staff members tried to build a vault at the very same moment, you could end up with two vaults, which must never happen. Making sure only one vault ever exists, even when many staff rush the door together, is exactly what thread-safe Singleton creation guarantees.

**One line to remember:** Singleton means one instance for the whole app, and in Java the safe, lazy, simple ways are the Bill Pugh holder idiom and the enum singleton.

sections.s2_technical:
Eager initialization creates the instance when the class loads: `private static final ConfigRegistry INSTANCE = new ConfigRegistry();`. It is inherently thread-safe because class initialization is done once by the JVM under a lock, and `getInstance()` just returns the field. The downside is it is not lazy; the instance is built even if never used, which wastes resources if construction is expensive.

Lazy with a synchronized getter builds the instance on first use and guards the whole method with a lock: `public static synchronized ConfigRegistry getInstance() { if (instance == null) instance = new ConfigRegistry(); return instance; }`. It is correct and lazy, but every single call acquires the lock even after the instance exists, which hurts performance under heavy concurrent reads.

Double-checked locking tries to lock only on the first creation. It checks for null without a lock, then locks and checks again: the field must be `volatile` so other threads see the fully constructed object. Without volatile, another thread could see a non-null reference pointing to a partially constructed object because of instruction reordering. The code is `if (instance == null) { synchronized(Lock.class) { if (instance == null) instance = new ConfigRegistry(); } }`. It is fast after initialization but error-prone to write correctly.

The Bill Pugh initialization-on-demand holder idiom uses a private static inner holder class. The outer class does not initialize the instance; the holder class is only loaded when `getInstance()` first references it, and class loading is thread-safe by the JVM. For example the holder has `static final ConfigRegistry INSTANCE = new ConfigRegistry();` and `getInstance()` returns `Holder.INSTANCE`. This is lazy, thread-safe, and requires no synchronization or volatile, which is why it is a top recommendation.

The enum singleton declares `enum ConfigRegistry { INSTANCE; ... }`. The JVM guarantees a single instance of each enum constant, and enums are automatically safe against serialization creating a second copy and against reflection attacks, which other approaches are not. Joshua Bloch in Effective Java calls the single-element enum the best way to implement a Singleton. Its only limitation is that an enum cannot extend a class.

A senior nuance: a real Singleton must also defend against cloning, serialization, and reflection creating a second instance. The enum handles all three for free, while the holder idiom needs a private constructor and, if serializable, a readResolve method. This is why for most cases I recommend the enum, and the Bill Pugh holder when I need to extend a class or have special construction needs.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India has a configuration registry that holds the current interest rates, fee schedules, and feature flags for the whole application.

Problem 1 — There must be exactly one registry. If two registries existed, one thread might read an old fee while another read a new fee, producing inconsistent charges to Rajesh. The whole point is a single shared source of truth, which is the Singleton pattern.

Problem 2 — Many threads start at once. At market open, dozens of request threads call getInstance at the same microsecond. If the creation is not thread-safe, two threads could both see null and both create a registry, defeating the purpose. This is why the construction must be thread-safe.

Problem 3 — Construction is a little expensive. Loading the fee schedule takes time, so we prefer lazy creation on first use rather than building it eagerly at startup if it might not be needed. This is why we care about lazy approaches.

Problem 4 — Attackers and frameworks can break naive singletons. Serialization and reflection can create a second instance behind your back. This is why the enum singleton, which blocks those, is attractive.

The demo implements the registry five ways, then launches many threads hitting getInstance simultaneously to prove each returns the same instance, and shows the enum approach as the clean final recommendation.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five Singleton implementations and 50 threads racing to fetch the holder instance.

Step 1: EagerConfig's instance was created the moment the class loaded, before main even ran. Calling getInstance twice returns the same reference, so the equality check prints true. The data, the single instance, already exists on the heap.

Step 2: SyncConfig.getInstance is called. The first call acquires the monitor lock, sees null, creates the instance, and returns it. The second call still acquires the lock, sees non-null, and returns the same instance. Both calls return the same object, but each paid the lock cost.

Step 3: DclConfig.getInstance is called. The first check sees null, enters the synchronized block, the second check also sees null, so it creates the instance into the volatile field. Because the field is volatile, any other thread that later sees a non-null reference is guaranteed to see a fully constructed object, never a half-built one.

Step 4: HolderConfig.getInstance references Holder.INSTANCE for the first time, which triggers the JVM to load and initialize the Holder class exactly once under the class-initialization lock. The instance is created lazily and safely with no synchronized keyword anywhere.

Step 5: Fifty tasks are submitted to a ten-thread pool, all calling HolderConfig.getInstance and recording the identity hash of what they got. Even though they race, the JVM's one-time class initialization guarantees they all receive the same object.

Step 6: The set of distinct identities is counted. It contains exactly one value, proving all 50 threads saw the single instance. No lock was written by us; the class loader provided the safety.

Step 7: The enum singleton EnumConfig.INSTANCE stores an equity fee rate and returns it, showing a Singleton used as real shared configuration. The enum guarantees one instance even against serialization and reflection.

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Five Singleton Implementations ═══

  ┌─ Approaches & trade-offs ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Eager:      simple, thread-safe, NOT lazy                  │
  │ Sync getter:lazy, but locks EVERY call (slow)              │
  │ DCL:        fast after init, needs volatile, tricky        │
  │ Bill Pugh:  lazy + safe via class load, no sync (PREFER)   │
  │ Enum:       concise, serialization/reflection safe (BEST)  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ Why volatile in DCL ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ instance = new DclConfig() is 3 steps: allocate, construct,│
  │ assign. Reordering can publish the ref before construct.   │
  │ volatile forbids that reorder → no partial object visible. │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ HolderConfig         │
  │ - HolderConfig()     │ private ctor
  │ + getInstance()      │──→ Holder.INSTANCE
  └─────────┬────────────┘
            │ owns (lazy)
            ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Holder (static)      │    │ EnumConfig           │
  │ + INSTANCE: Holder   │    │ INSTANCE             │
  │   Config (final)     │    │ - equityFeeRate      │
  └──────────────────────┘    │ + get/setFeeRate()   │
                              └──────────────────────┘

  ── Defenses a real singleton needs ──────────────────────────
  Cloning:       enum blocks it; others override clone() to throw
  Serialization: enum safe; others need readResolve()
  Reflection:    enum safe; others: throw in ctor if instance set
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Singleton pattern ensures a class has exactly one instance for the whole application and gives a single global access point to it. The hard part in Java is making sure that when many threads call getInstance at the same moment, they cannot accidentally create two instances, so I always talk about thread safety.

There are five common ways. Eager initialization creates the instance in a static final field when the class loads; it is inherently thread-safe because the JVM initializes a class once under a lock, but it is not lazy, so it wastes resources if the instance is never used. The synchronized getter is lazy and correct, but it locks on every single call even after the instance exists, which hurts performance under heavy reads. Double-checked locking checks for null without a lock, then locks and checks again, and it must use a volatile field; without volatile, instruction reordering can publish a reference to a partially constructed object that another thread sees as non-null, which is a subtle and dangerous bug.

The two I prefer are the Bill Pugh holder idiom and the enum. The Bill Pugh idiom puts the instance in a private static inner holder class, so the instance is created only when getInstance first touches the holder, and the JVM's one-time class initialization makes it both lazy and thread-safe with no synchronized keyword and no volatile. The enum singleton declares a single enum constant, and the JVM guarantees one instance; crucially the enum is also safe against serialization and reflection creating a second copy, which the other approaches are not, so Joshua Bloch calls it the best way to implement a Singleton. Its only limitation is that an enum cannot extend a class.

In my work at the National Bank of India this matters for the shared configuration registry that holds interest rates, fee schedules, and feature flags, where two instances could make one thread charge an old fee while another charges a new one. For that I use the enum when I just need one instance with no inheritance, and the Bill Pugh holder when I need a private constructor with special construction logic. I also remember that a JVM singleton is one per JVM, so across a cluster the real source of truth has to be a shared store like a database or Redis, not just the in-memory singleton, and mentioning that distinction is what shows I understand it beyond the textbook.
